title: Ritual and Home Practice
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley shares how reading Paula Arai's book "Bringing Zen Home" has inspired them to incorporate body rituals into their daily life, such as cleaning and flower arranging, which they believe help cultivate compassion and well-being. These practices are rooted in Buddhist teachings and have become an integral part of their meditation practice at home. By embracing these simple yet profound rituals, Seishu has found a deeper sense of connection with themselves, others, and even those who have passed away, bringing peace and unity to their relationships. This newfound awareness has also helped them cultivate gratitude and become more mindful of their actions' impact on others.
topics: disciplining the body to manifest true nature

sentences.text: I was going to give a series of talks on koans, but I felt like I needed a little more time to work with it in my day-to-day life, so I'm going to postpone a talk on this particular koan.
Instead, I'm going to talk about some reading that I have done recently that's really energized my practice, especially at home.

A couple of months ago, I looked at my bookcase and I saw quite a few Buddhist books that I've had for a number of years that have not been touched, and I thought, I'm going to make an effort in the next several months to read some of these books.
The first one that I picked has been really interesting.

It's called *Bringing Zen Home: The Healing Heart of Japanese Women's Rituals* by Paula Arai, and I think I went to Japan in May with some other people, and I think that trip really stirred my interest in this book.
Paula Arai is a Buddhist scholar.
She has a PhD from Harvard in Buddhist studies, and she's a professor of religious studies at Louisiana State University.
She was in the Northwest, I think, seven or eight years ago down on Vashon Island giving a talk.
I think she had done the research for this book, but hadn't written it yet, and I know Jeff McKenna went down to hear her, and someone else from the Sangha did too, and I don't remember.
I remember hearing a little bit about her work several years ago.
This is her second book on Zen practice in Japan.
For this one, she spent twelve years following a dozen women in Japan and looking at their ritual practice.

What Zen Buddhist rituals do they use in their day-to-day lives to handle the biggest challenges that they face, which include chronic illness, death and illness of aging parents and other family members, traumatic histories, some of the women were children during World War II, and chronic pain, things like that.
In our Soto Zen practice in America, we really emphasize meditation, but we do have rituals.
However, in Japan, meditation isn't practiced as widely, at least outside of monasteries, and the practices described here are all ritual.
The women, as far as I know, did virtually no meditation.

It's really interesting to read about how powerful and effective these rituals have been in helping these practitioners, and they're all lay practitioners—there are no priests, no residents of monasteries—and how much the rituals have helped them in their day-to-day lives.
The women she studied range in age from mid-forties to mid-seventies.
Most of them have been either married or widowed.
Many of them have adult children; a few were not married and did not have children.
About half of them had careers, so she covered kind of a full range of lifestyles.

The kind of rituals that she studied and writes about in the book are rituals performed for health and home safety, for the well-being of family members, rituals to nurture the self, rituals to create and appreciate beauty, like flower arranging, tea service, taking walks in nature, and also rituals to honor deceased family members.
It's that category of ritual that was most interesting to me and actually has most impacted my practice at home, and I'll talk more about that in a few minutes.

In the book, Paula Arai often quotes or refers to Eihei Dogen's writings, and for those of you who are new, he was a Japanese priest who lived from twelve hundred to twelve fifty-two, I believe, and is considered the founder of Soto Zen, which is the style of Buddhism that we practice.
We often read his writings and try to understand them, and he's considered a really important contributor to our practice.
What she said is really interesting.

She said that Dogen took the common phrase mind-body and switched it to body-mind, because he believed that in order to realize our true nature, Buddha nature, it's most effective to discipline and train the body.
If the body moves and acts in accordance with respect and non-waste and treats everything as part of one integrated whole, then the mind will naturally experience compassion, according to Dogen.
You can think wonderful thoughts, but if your body doesn't act accordingly, your true nature is not manifested.
So these rituals in the book are all body rituals.
Even something as day-to-day as cleaning can be done in this way, if you use full mind and body attention.
Paula Arai came up with a great phrase that I really like, and she said, "polishing the floor polishes the heart."
One woman with extreme chronic hip pain found great comfort in a monthly ritual of using brush and ink to copy the Heart Sutra, and she would do this at her local Zen monastery.
Another woman in the group was told in her mid-sixties that she had cancer in her abdomen, and it was beyond medical treatment.
There was nothing more that medicine could do for her.

So she was given a couple of standard cleaning cloths by the abbess of her local Zen monastery, and these cloths had the abbess's calligraphy on them and also a figure with hands in gassho, which is a symbol of gratitude.
The woman believed firmly that these cloths would heal her, so she did a ritual a couple of times a day.
She would put one cloth on her pillow and lay down on the pillow, put the other cloth on her abdomen at the site of her cancer.
Ten years later, she was living a healthy lifestyle and had no sign of cancer.

As I said earlier, the rituals that really stirred my interest were the ones involving deceased relatives, and in Japan they have a lot of rituals for people who have died recently and even in the past.
They have a ritual right at the time of death, and these often involve candles and incense and offering tea.

They have a ritual at the one-week anniversary, at the one-month anniversary, at the one-year, two-year, three-year anniversary, and they also have an annual festival in the summer called Obon, which is a festival for honoring the spirits of relatives.
Many people in Japan return to the site of their ancestors' graves, and they'll clean the grave and offer incense and tea and things like that.
It's a very popular festival, and it seems like in Japan there's much more of a relationship with ancestors than we have here in the West.
According to the book, deceased relatives are considered personal Buddhas for the loved ones who are still alive, and a relationship is maintained on that basis.
Many homes in Japan have an altar with not only a Buddha on it, but pictures of relatives.
When we were in Kyoto, there are just many, many shops that just sell altars and Buddhas and all kinds of things used for ritual.
There must have been a dozen of them, and they're all doing good business, so it's very popular in Japan, very common.
I wanted to give you a couple of examples from the book of the kinds of rituals that Paula Arai found.
The first one involves a woman by the name of Honda-san, and she comes back to her studio apartment.
Every time she comes home, she opens the door and cries out, "I'm home."
She's using a particular phrase that's a common family greeting reserved for those coming in or going out of the home, but she lives alone.
She's addressing the photos of her parents on her homemade altar.
Her parents died more than thirty years previously, and yet they are still considered her family.
Her heart hears their response, "Your return home is welcomed."
When Paula interviewed her, she talked about why she does this.
She said, "I feel like I'm not alone.
In my home, I have my parents' pictures.
I give flowers, water, and food.
When I leave, I ask them to take care of the house, and I say that I'm leaving and I will be back.
I have not felt a sense of loneliness."
So that's one of the rituals.
The other one is from Paula Arai herself.
It's this particular event that inspired her to do the research for this book and then write the book.
I'm just going to tell you a little bit about the situation, then I'll just read what she wrote about her experience.
She had been caring for her ill mother for a number of years, and she was getting help from a non-in-Japan keto sensei.
Her mother had just died.
*Hands shaking, I cleared the bedside table of the vials of morphine sponges and salves.
The ultimacy of the moment engulfed me.
How was I to ensure my mother's passage through the perilous transition?
Keto sensei had encouraged me to call her.
The elderly Zen nun had helped my mother and me through the last nine years, applying her healing balm of compassion.
It was the middle of the night in Japan, but I knew that at three forty-five in the morning, she would be at her temple.
The telephone in my hand was a lifeline.
I knew intellectually about Soto Zen rituals that recognize the deceased as a Buddha.
But it was keto sensei in her unheated worship hall ten thousand miles away who guided me through these first terrifying, disorienting moments.*
Trusting her to know what to do, I followed her instructions for the ritual of safely sending off the deceased on her journey of death.

Frantic to treat our new Buddha properly, I rushed to find the bronze plum blossom incense burner, the sandalwood incense sticks, white candle and plain carved wooden figure of Kannon, the goddess of compassion.
Not more than ten minutes after my mother breathed her last, the bedside table was transformed into a mortuary altar.
As I offered a stick of incense in her honor, I saw my mother's face take on the peace that I have seen so often on images of Buddha.
Our relationship was transforming before my very eyes.
When I placed the incense in the burner, I became one with all who had done so before.
In the moment that had threatened to be the loneliest of my life, I instead experienced a profound connection with all grievers past and future.
I was not alone.
I was united with everyone who had lost a loved one.
Keto sensei had guided us through this critical transition with the wisdom that transcended barriers of space, time, life and death.
At that moment, the healing power of ritual became a visceral reality.
Because of these kinds of stories, I thought that I would add some relatives to my home altar.
I put pictures of my father, his sister, my Aunt Marie, his brother, my Uncle John, and my wife, Carolyn's brother, Butch.
I actually brought pictures with me, and you can pass them around if you want.
I'll just tell you a little bit about each one of these people.
My father died in two thousand two at the age of ninety, and he was a remarkable guy.
He was kind and funny and he had great equanimity.
I don't remember him ever getting angry when he drove the car.
We would be in a traffic jam or somebody would do something reckless, and he did.
He never laid on his horn and never yelled.
It seems to me if you're going to lose it, that's one of the places you would.
That certainly had been true for me, but he never did that.
He treated everybody with respect.
Even when he was dying, he was usually cheerful and he almost never complained.
He was calm.
I remember being around him at the end and I thought, I want to be like that when my time comes.
My Aunt Marie, his sister, died in two thousand three at the age of ninety-three of longevity on that side of the family.
She lived most of her life in New York City, so we didn't see much of her when I was a kid.
I remember her as a smart, sophisticated, and in a good way, eccentric person.
She had a job.
She worked at Macy's in Manhattan.
She ran a whole floor and was a buyer, and she didn't like her job at all.
When she was fifty, she quit and she went back to school and got an MSW, a master's in social work.
Then she started doing mental health work at one of the community mental health centers in New York City.
I remember I talked with her on the phone from time to time, and I was just finishing a degree in economics.
I'd listen to her talk about her work and I thought, God, that work sounds really interesting, but I just had to finish and get out of school.
I didn't want to be in school any longer.
So I finished my degree and I worked a couple of years as an economic analyst at a bank, and I didn't like it.
So I quit and I got an MSW and started doing mental health work.
That was what I did for most of my career.
I think in part inspired by her example, my uncle John was killed in World War Two in nineteen forty-four.
I never met him; I was named after him.
I was born a few years after he died.
He and my dad were very close.
About thirty years ago, I had a very interesting experience.
Carolyn and I were talking to some friends, and they were telling us about seeing a psychic in Bellingham.
It was a really interesting experience, and you should go, they said.
So we made an appointment with this woman.
I remember when we both heard each other's what you call an appointment with a psychic.
I guess we'd heard what she said to each of us.
But she took my watch and she held it in her hand for a little while.
Then she just started to talk about what came up for her, and she said that she was picking up that I had a spirit kind of hovering around me.
It was a spirit that had been around me for a long time, for many, many years.
I can remember everything she said, but she asked, "Well, what do you think of that?"
I said, "Well, I don't know.
I'd never had the feeling that some spirit was hovering around me."
But I told her that I was named after my uncle who had died in World War Two.
Then she paused a little bit, and then she started to say what he was like as a person, described while he was this way and that way, and then what he liked, the kinds of things he was interested in.
I don't remember any of that.
But I do remember a couple of weeks after that, visiting my parents and telling my dad about this, about this appointment.
I repeated what she said about Uncle John, and as I was describing it to him, he kept saying, "That's right.
That's right.
How did she know that?"
That was pretty interesting.
I never, like I said, I never had the feeling that a spirit was hovering around me, but I really like the idea of it, and I hope it's true.
They say in Buddhism that our ability to sense reality with our senses gives us a very narrow view of reality.
They use the phrase, "the way is vast and wide."
So maybe I had his spirit around me.
I like it.
I like that idea anyway.
The last person on the altar is my brother-in-law, Butch.
He died in nineteen ninety-nine.
He had brain cancer, and he was really a neat guy.
He was really energetic.
He was interested in all kinds of things.
He was a good musician and an athlete.
He was planning to move to Bellingham.
He lived in Southern California when he retired and he died, instead of retiring.
But he was really close with my wife; they were really close their whole lives.
Carolyn said they were joined at the heart.
So his death was really hard on her, and it still is.
But he was a good guy to put on the altar.
I can't put into words or describe what difference it makes to have these people on the altar, but it really does seem to make a difference.
I like having them there.
I seem to look forward to meditating more than I used to.

I almost never miss a morning meditation, and I reflect on their lives more than I used to, what their lives were like, and I feel much gratitude for not only what they've all given to me, but what they contributed to the members of our family.
It's really given me a lot more gratitude, and gratitude has been something that I've really tried to work on in my practice for the last couple of years.
I really appreciate having this kind of addition to it, and I recommend the practice of putting your relatives on the altar.
On the subject of gratitude, I just have one other little thing I want to say.
This is a different topic.
About a month ago, Jaren, who's not here tonight as a member of our group, sent me an article on a method of self-reflection called Naikan.
It's spelled N-A-I-K-A-N, almost sounds like the camera.
It's a Japanese word that means looking inside, or expressed more poetically, seeing oneself with the mind's eye.
It was developed in Japan in the nineteen forties by a priest by the name of Ishin Yoshimoto, who was a Buddhist in the Pure Land sect.
Apparently, there are a number of Naikan centers in Japan and Europe and some in America that teach this method of self-reflection, and they ask people to ask three questions.
You can apply these questions to anything.
You can apply it to a person like you're in a relationship with.
You can apply it to a job or a project.
I've been applying it to time, like today or this week.
The questions are: what have I received from the person or the job or whatever?
What have I given to you?
And the third one is, what trouble and difficulties have I caused?
So again, you can apply these three questions to anything.
It's been really interesting to do that.
I am prone to spending too much time thinking about what I want, what I haven't received enough of, that kind of thing.
It's really great to ask, "What have I given today?"
Or even, "What opportunities did I have to give today?
Did I even notice them?
How did I respond?"
And always, of course, a good thing to ask, "What troubles have I caused?
What problems have I caused today?"
It's especially a good thing to do if you're married or in a relationship to keep that one in mind.
I'm really appreciating kind of working with these three questions.
Reflect on these three questions at the end of the day has been a really neat practice.
I'm sorry Jaren's not here, so I can't thank him in person for sending me the article, but it's been another thing that's kind of helped with my gratitude practice.
That's really what I wanted to talk about tonight: just to share with you the reading I've done recently and how it's impacted my practice.
Thank you very much for being here and for listening tonight.
